title: The Man Who Made the Pouch

pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 50. Bowls sold: 88. Mr. Tsai's shop: closing. Ama's mood: (she would not let me write it).*

The lane was dressed for the New Year. Red banners hung from every stall, and the lanterns had been doubled, making the light thick and golden, like a jar of honey tipped over the street. People wore their new clothes, and the air smelled of roasted peanuts mixed with the sharp bite of cold wind.

Stall nineteen was busy. I ladled the soup while Ama stood with her wrist in a white brace. She was not cooking; she was supervising.

"Yun-Lin, the scallions are too long!" she shouted over the noise.

"They are exactly as I cut them," I said.

"They are decorative, not edible!"

I cut them shorter. I did not argue. It was strange to see her standing still, because without the pot steaming in front of her, she looked smaller, like a doll pulled from a box. But her voice was still the boss. It filled the lane, pushing back the cold. By ten o'clock, I had written eighty-eight in the ledger. It was a good number. It was enough.
pages.image: A bustling night market lane at night, filled with red banners and glowing lanterns, showing a small girl in a checked apron ladling soup while an elderly woman in a wrist brace stands nearby shouting, with customers in new clothes in the background. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
The rush settled into a hum. The steam rose, and the lanterns swayed. I was wiping a table when I saw him.

Mr. Tsai shuffled toward us. He wore his thick cardigan and his glasses were smudged. In his pocket, the wooden beads of his abacus clacked softly. He stopped at our counter. He did not look at the soup. He looked at the counter.

He took a small cloth pouch from his pocket and set it down. It smelled of earth and dried fruit.

"This is the last one," he said. His voice was slow and quiet. "I am eighty-four. My hands are tired. My son wants me to come to the city. To live with them." He touched the pouch, then pulled his hand back. "The shop closes at the end of the month."

The noise of the market seemed to drop away. The steam curled around his words.
pages.image: An elderly spice merchant in a cardigan and thick glasses stands at a stall counter, placing a small cloth pouch on the wooden surface, with a steaming pot and a young girl in an apron watching him closely.

pages.text:
Ama stood perfectly still, her eyes locked on the small pouch resting on the counter. She did not reach for it immediately. Instead, her free hand, the one not trapped in the brace, drifted forward until her fingers brushed the rough cloth. She kept her hand there, as if expecting it to dissolve into the steam.

"Forty years," she said. Her voice dropped so low that only the three of us could hear it. "You never mentioned you were stopping."

Mr. Tsai adjusted his smudged glasses, his movements slow and careful. "I did not know how to say it."

Ama looked up. Her eyes were bright and sharp.

"You just did."

She did not pick up the pouch, nor did she tuck it away. She simply turned back to the great pot, her shoulders remaining stiff and high.

I watched her hand. It was trembling, just a little, like a loose leaf caught in a draft. I had never seen her tremble before. I wanted to say something, to fix it, but there was nothing to fix. There was only the pouch, the silence, and the heavy scent of star anise hanging in the cold air.
pages.image: An elderly woman in a floral vest holds a small cloth pouch in her hand, her expression serious and quiet, while an old man in a cardigan stands nearby, with steam rising from a pot behind them.

pages.text:
Later, after the last customer left and the plastic stools were stacked upside down on the tables, I wiped the counter. The wood was cold against my palm, a sharp, clean chill that seemed to travel up my wrist.

"Ama," I said, not looking up from the rag. "What will happen to the soup? Without the pouches?"

She was drying the ladle. She dried it slowly, her hand moving in long, deliberate circles that made a soft *shhk* against the metal. "I will find another spice shop," she said, her voice flat and final.

"No one makes it like Mr. Tsai," I said, dropping the rag on the counter. "The blend is different. It is the heart. It’s like trying to eat cereal with a fork. It’s all wrong."

Ama stopped drying. She looked at the ladle, then she looked at me, her eyes wide and serious.

"I know," she said.

It was the first time I had ever heard her sound afraid. It was a small, quiet sound, like the river behind our house changing course in the night. I looked at the pouch on the counter. It sat there, waiting. I did not know what to do or say, so I just wiped the counter, over and over, until the wood was shiny and reflected the dim light of the lanterns.
pages.image: A small girl in a green jacket wipes a wooden counter with a cloth, looking at an elderly woman who is drying a ladle, with a small pouch of spices sitting on the counter between them.

pages.text:
I picked up the cloth pouch and untied the knot. Inside were tiny things: star anise, dark and sharp; cinnamon bark, curled and brown; fennel seeds, pale and sweet; a single peppercorn, black and hard; a piece of licorice root, dark and rough; tangerine peel, dried and orange; a bay leaf, green and thin; and a clove, small and brown.

Eight things.

I held them in my palm, feeling how they were light, yet somehow heavy. If I knew exactly what was in it, and Mr. Tsai knew how much, then maybe.

I took my pencil from behind my ear and opened my spiral notebook. I wrote: ASK MR. TSAI.

Ama was humming, oblivious to my thoughts. I added one more line below the first. DON'T TELL AMA YET.

Then I closed the notebook, tucked it into my pocket, and looked at the pouch one last time before putting it back in the cloth.
pages.image: A close-up of a girl's hand holding a small open cloth pouch filled with dried spices and herbs, including star anise and cinnamon, with a spiral notebook and pencil visible in the background.
